title: Why 536 Was the Worst Year to Be Alive
description:
In 536 AD, the sun went dark for 18 months. Crops failed, snow fell in summer, and famine swept the ancient world. Scientists now call it the worst year to be alive — here is the real story, from eyewitness accounts to ice-core science.

Chapters:
0:00 The sun went out
0:44 Witnesses around the world
1:31 Ice cores: the smoking gun
2:21 Tree rings: the coldest summer
3:06 The second eruption of 540
3:46 Famine: when the harvest died
4:44 The Plague of Justinian
5:27 A century of cold
6:33 The volcano that vanished
7:02 The year the sun went out

Honestly, what amazes me most is that one volcano, half a world away, could bring entire civilizations to their knees — no war, no invasion, just ash and a dimmed sun.

Sources:
- Gibbons, A. (2018). "Eruption made 536 'the worst year to be alive'." Science, 362(6416), 733–734.
- Sigl, M. et al. (2015). "Timing and climate forcing of volcanic eruptions for the past 2,500 years." Nature, 523, 543–549.
- Büntgen, U. et al. (2016). "Cooling and societal change during the Late Antique Little Ice Age from 536 to around 660 AD." Nature Geoscience, 9, 231–236.
- Larsen, L.B. et al. (2008). "New ice core evidence for a volcanic cause of the A.D. 536 dust veil." Geophysical Research Letters, 35(4).
- Harper, K. (2017). The Fate of Rome. Princeton University Press.
- Procopius, History of the Wars (trans. H.B. Dewing, Loeb).
